Stiff-Person Syndrome Presenting as Eating Disorder:
A Case Report
Miroslav Cuturic, MD1,2*
Laurie M. Harden, MD 2
Melissa H. Kannaday, MD 2
Nioaka N. Campbell, MD 2
Richard K. Harding, MD 2
ABSTRACT
Objective: To report a case of a 35-
year-old female initially treated for ano-
rexia nervosa who was found to have
Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS).
Method: Case report.
Results: The patient reported panic
attacks at meal times that were found to
consist of tetanic contractions of the axial
musculature. Swallowing initiated reﬂex-
ive painful muscle spasms that conse-
quently resulted in cibophobia and sig-
niﬁcant weight loss. Her serum tested
positive for anti-glutamic acid decarboxy-
lase antibodies, and she subsequently
improved with appropriate treatment for
SPS.
Discussion: SPS has not been previ-
ously reported in the context of eating
disorders, although it has been linked to
other psychiatric disorders. Often the
psychiatrist may be the ﬁrst physician to
diagnose SPS. We present this case to
alert practitioners to the potential co-
morbidity and symptom overlap between
SPS and eating disorders, to aid in
early recognition and appropriate treat-
ment of this rare illness. VVC 2010 by Wiley
Periodicals, Inc.
Keywords: Stiff-Person syndrome;
anorexia; eating disorders; depression;
anxiety
(Int J Eat Disord 2011; 44:284–286)
Introduction
Eating disorders often present a diagnostic chal-
lenge as patients may deny or minimize their symp-
toms when being assessed.
1 In addition, other
comorbidities such as depression or anxiety disor-
ders may further complicate the diagnostic pro-
cess.
2,3 Weight loss is not limited to eating disorders
and may be seen in other psychiatric disorders such
as depression, conversion disorder, schizophrenia,
and speciﬁc phobias.
3 As with all psychiatric evalu-
ations, care must be taken to rule out organic
causes of symptoms. The diagnostic challenge
becomes increasingly difﬁcult when the possible
organic cause is rare and not evident with routine
laboratory testing or diagnostic interviewing.
We report a case of a female patient initially
treated for anorexia nervosa, depression, and anxi-
ety who was found, in fact, to have stiff-person syn-
drome (SPS).
Case Report
A 35-year-old woman with a longstanding history
of hypothyroidism and borderline noninsulin de-
pendent diabetes mellitus (Type 2) was referred by
a local mental health center to our psychiatric hos-
pital for an inpatient evaluation and treatment of
anorexia nervosa, depression, and anxiety disorder.
She had a 2-year history of increasing resistance
toward food intake, citing anxiety, and fear of food
(cibophobia). Although, she had been receiving
outpatient psychotherapy for depression and anxi-
ety disorder, she continued to refuse food. Her
weight declined to a body mass index (BMI) of 12.5
(normal 18.5–24.9), at which point she was referred
for inpatient psychiatric treatment of anorexia
nervosa.
Prior evaluations included a metabolic and endo-
crinologic work-up, magnetic resonance imaging of
the brain, electroencephalogram (EEG), nerve con-
duction studies, electromyography, modiﬁed bar-
ium swallow studies, and muscle biopsy, all of
which were reported to be normal. Her electrolytes,
liver function tests, thyroid function tests, blood
glucose, and glycosylated hemoglobin were also
assessed and found to be within normal limits.
Accepted 5 November 2009
1 South Carolina Department of Mental Health, Columbia, South
Carolina

2 Department of Neuropsychiatry and Behavioral Science,

South Carolina

CASE REPORT

On admission she appeared cachectic with con-
stricted affect. She reported ‘‘fair’’ mood. Her
thought process was coherent and devoid of any
delusions, hallucinations, suicidal or homicidal
ideation. She did not perceive herself overweight or
underweight and did not express any concern
about her body appearance. She reported a ‘‘fear of
food’’ and described ‘‘panic attacks’’ preceding
every meal, consisting of anxiety and a choking
sensation, with pain throughout her body. She also
reported that the ‘‘panic attacks’’ could be elicited
by loud noises or stress, which led to a secluded
lifestyle of limited daily activities and self-care.
Her vital signs were normal, except for a BMI of
12.5 (weight of 30.8 kg, height 157 cm). Her physi-
cal and neurological exams were within normal
range, except for moderately increased tone in the
lower extremities. There was notable hyper-erect
and upright body posture with ambulation. Her
medications included sertraline 50 mg daily and
levothyroxine 25 mcg daily.
The following day at breakfast, she developed an
episode of ongoing generalized opistotonic postur-
ing, requiring an urgent neurological consultation.
She was found supine on the sofa, profusely dia-
phoretic, alert and fearful. She was able to establish
eye contact but unable to verbalize secondary to
trismus. She was able to grip on request but was
otherwise immobile due to extension posturing
with simultaneous continuous tetanic contraction
of the agonist and antagonist muscles in the limbs
and axial musculature, preventing any passive or
active motion in the joints. There was no clonic or
myoclonic activity. Her pupils were equally round
and reactive to light. Her vital signs revealed a tem-
perature of 36.8 degrees Celsius, rapid shallow res-
pirations at 32 breaths per minute and a pulse of
145 beats per minute. Within 15 min after receiving
lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly and 2 L/min oxy-
gen via nasal cannula, her tetanic contractions
gradually receded.
Subsequently, she reported a complete recollec-
tion of the event and explained that the episode
represented her typical ‘‘panic attack.’’ Intact cog-
nition in the context of a generalized motor spell
excluded the possibility of a seizure, particularly
taking into consideration prior negative EEG and
neuroimaging evaluations. However, as she had
never reported a fear of gaining weight, the cardi-
nal symptom of an eating disorder, we suspected
an underlying organic etiology for her weight
loss. Based on the physical exam and ﬁndings
during the observed episode, we believed that her
attacks may represent episodes of continuous
muscle activity such as seen in tetanus or SPS.
The chronic course of the condition, well-docu-
mented tetanus immunization records, and lack
of any recent penetrating injuries ruled out fur-
ther consideration of tetanus. Her serum sample
was tested for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase
(anti-GAD) antibodies, and found positive at 183
lg/mL (normal less than 0.05 lg/mL), thus sup-
porting the diagnosis of SPS.
She was started on clonazepam 1 mg twice daily
and gabapentin 300 mg three times daily for mus-
cle spasms and anxiety. Sertraline was replaced
with mirtazapine 15 mg each evening. Her diet was
gradually advanced as she reported mild ameliora-
tion of her spasms and better tolerance of oral
intake. Within a week, she was discharged home to
follow-up with her neurologist and psychiatrist. A
referral to a movement disorder clinic was made

for further management of SPS.
Over the next several months, she was treated by
a nutritionist and underwent both physical and
speech therapy. In addition, gabapentin was
increased to 600 mg three times daily, and baclofen
was added at 10 mg three times daily. Subsequently,
she was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin
(IVIg) infusions for SPS. On her one year follow-up
visit, her BMI had improved to 17.6, and she
reported signiﬁcant alleviation of her spasms, anxi-
ety, and depression.
Discussion
SPS is a rare autoimmune neurological disorder
characterized by progressive muscle stiffness, rigid-
ity, and spasm involving the axial and facial muscu-
lature, resulting in severely impaired ambulation
and disability.
4,5 Two distinctive variants of SPS are
known, the paraneoplastic and idiopathic forms. 6
The former is associated with amphiphysin
antibodies. The latter, as seen in our patient, is
associated with elevated anti-GAD antibodies.
6
Neuroimaging and EEG are mostly unremarkable
in this condition.
7 Electromyography usually shows
continuous motor unit activity, but may also be
normal in the early stages, particularly if the para-
spinal muscles are not tested, as was the case in
our patient.
7
In the idiopathic form of SPS, anti-GAD antibod-
ies are felt to play a role in gamma-aminobutyric
acid (GABA) dysfunction, through mechanisms still
not fully elucidated.
4–8 Glutamic acid (GA), the pre-
cursor molecule, is converted to GABA by the
action of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD).
8,9 It is
theorized that anti-GAD antibodies may inhibit

GAD function, and therefore limit the conversion
of GA to GABA. 8,9 Evidence suggests that autoanti-
bodies may be directed against different isoforms
of GAD. This may explain clinical polymorphism of
SPS and the presence of anti-GAD antibodies in
disorders unrelated to SPS, such as Type 1 diabetes
mellitus and thyroiditis.
9
GABA is a principal inhibitory neurotransmitter
in the central nervous system, necessary for normal
neuro-behavioral functioning. 10 It is reported that
between 30% and 50% of all central synapses are
GABAergic, with dopaminergic, noradrenergic and
serotonergic neurons all being under inhibitory
control by GABA.
10 Dysfunction of GABA inhibition
has been implicated in many diseases including
epilepsy, SPS, anxiety disorders, schizophrenia,
premenstrual dysphoric disorder, drug addiction
and depression. 8–10 Indeed, the GABA dysfunction
present in SPS patients may contribute to the for-
mation of independently diagnosable psychiatric
disorders such as anxiety and depressive disor-
ders.
8–10 Our case highlights the confounding
implications of GABA related diseases with overlap-
ping symptomatology.
It has been proposed that in SPS, anti-GAD anti-
bodies inhibit GABA production which conse-
quently lowers the threshold for both anxiety disor-
ders and muscle spasms.
11,12 Although it has not
been reported in the context of eating disorders,
SPS has been reported in association with speciﬁc
phobia, particularly task-speciﬁc phobia and avoid-
ance of situations related to the motor symptoms.
13
It is likely that in our patient reﬂexive painful mus-
cle spasms precipitated by swallowing resulted in
cibophobia and consequent weight loss.
Many individuals, before being diagnosed with
SPS, may carry a diagnosis of a psychogenic or hys-
terical movement disorder. 14 The distinction from
psychiatric illness is made even more difﬁcult by
the pattern of exacerbation of muscle spasms sec-
ondary to emotional upset, unexpected noise or
tactile stimuli. In addition, the frequent correlation
between signiﬁcant life events and onset of SPS
symptoms complicate the diagnostic process.
14
The majority of patients have both facial and tho-
racic musculature involvement, which can lead to
episodes of breathing or swallowing difﬁculties that
may be interpreted as panic attacks.
4 Conse-
quently, patients with SPS are often referred for
psychiatric evaluation, and the psychiatrist may be
the ﬁrst physician to diagnose SPS.
12,14,15
The treatment of SPS consists primarily of
symptomatic care with benzodiazepines and/or
muscle relaxants such as baclofen. 4,7 Other
options include antiepileptic medications, partic-
ularly gabapentin. 7,16 Immunomodulation with
intravenous immunoglobulins is one of the few
modalities that demonstrated beneﬁt in a double-
blinded, randomized controlled trial.
16 Psychiatric
treatment is beneﬁcial in cases with superimposed
anxiety, alcohol abuse or depression.
12–15 In addi-
tion to pharmacotherapy and immunomodula-
tion, our case of SPS with prominent weight loss,
depression and anxiety required a multidiscipli-
nary approach. The interdisciplinary team
involved psychiatry, neurology, nutrition, physical
and speech therapy.
We present this case to alert care providers to the
potential comorbidity and symptom overlap
between SPS, eating disorders and mental illness,
aiding in the early recognition and appropriate
treatment of this rare disorder.
